title: Markov Chains & Hidden Markov Models
html:
To reason over time, model the world as a sequence of states where the future depends only on the present. When the states themselves are hidden and only noisy observations are seen, you get a hidden Markov model (HMM).

Markov assumption — the next state depends only on the current state: P(Xₜ | X₀…Xₜ₋₁) = P(Xₜ | Xₜ₋₁). With a fixed transition matrix the process is stationary and is a Markov chain.

Hidden Markov models

An HMM adds a sensor model P(Eₜ | Xₜ). The textbook umbrella world: a guard underground can't see the weather, only whether the director brings an umbrella. Rain persists with probability 0.7; the umbrella appears on 90% of rainy days and 20% of dry days.

TaskComputesAlgorithm
FilteringP(Xₜ | e₁:ₜ) — belief about nowForward algorithm
PredictionP(Xₜ₊ₖ | e₁:ₜ) — the futureForward, then transitions only
SmoothingP(Xₖ | e₁:ₜ), k < t — the past, with hindsightForward–backward
Most likely explanationargmax P(x₁:ₜ | e₁:ₜ) — the best state sequenceViterbi (dynamic programming)
LearningTransition and sensor models from dataBaum–Welch (EM)
Key point

Before deep learning, HMMs powered speech recognition, part-of-speech tagging and gene finding. The same filtering idea with continuous states and Gaussian noise is the Kalman filter (tracking, GPS, robotics); with samples it is the particle filter (robot localisation).

What is the Markov assumption?

The future is conditionally independent of the past given the present state: P(Xₜ | X₀:ₜ₋₁) = P(Xₜ | Xₜ₋₁). It keeps models of time compact; if it doesn't hold, enrich the state (add more history or variables).

What problems does an HMM solve, and with which algorithms?

Filtering (forward algorithm), prediction, smoothing (forward–backward), the most likely hidden-state sequence (Viterbi), and learning the parameters (Baum–Welch / EM). Each runs in time linear in the sequence length.
